# Three stationary tetrahedral sections in one pencil, and their exact funded curvature

This note has two conclusions. First, the proposed claim that a fixed tetrahedral centroid and a fixed 2+2 split admit at most two stationary sections in one pencil is false. There are three pairwise distinct sections in the exact rational family below. Second, their associated three-full-row stochastic configuration is nevertheless a strict saddle: a positive capacity variation in one row exceeds the exact optimal curvature cost of funding it from the other two rows. This is a proved family, not a classification of every stationary three-row configuration.

## 1. An actual one-parameter pencil with a common section centroid

Choose 0<p<1/3 and put

    q=(1-p)/(1+3p), s=p+q.

Then p<q, 2/3<s<1, and pq=(1-s)/3. Rational p gives rational values throughout. Consider the three raw tetrahedral cap margin vectors

    c_1=(p,q,-1,-1),
    c_2=(q,p,-1,-1),
    c_3=(-s,-s,2,2).                                 (1)

They sum to zero and are pairwise nonproportional. All have the same unoriented split {1,2}|{3,4}; the first two capture the first pair, while the third captures the second. Their actual section centroids all equal

    b=(A,A,C,C), A=1/(s+2), C=s/[2(s+2)].            (2)

Here A>1/3, whereas C<1/3. One exact verification uses the quadrilateral centroid formula. For c_1 the diagonal coordinates are (1/p,1/q,1,1). The relation 3pq+p+q=1 is equivalent to

    (1/p-1)(1/q-1)=4.

Substitution into the four actual section-centroid coordinates gives (2). Swapping p,q gives the same vector for c_2. For c_3 the equal positive and equal negative heights give the section-product centroid (A,A,C,C) directly. Equivalently, its positive-coordinate sum is s/(s+2), and both pair splits are uniform. Thus all three planes pass through b and have their section centroids there.

These three normals lie in the two-dimensional pencil spanned by c_1,c_2, and are distinct even after identifying opposite orientations. Therefore both fixed-split uniqueness and an at-most-two-in-pencil assertion fail for actual tetrahedral sections. No stochastic optimality is asserted from stationarity alone.

## 2. Exact cap fractions and positive stochastic rows

For raw margins (p,q,-r,-w), p,q,r,w>0, the captured fraction is

    P=[p^2q^2+pq(p+q)(r+w)+(p^2+pq+q^2)rw]
                          /[(p+r)(p+w)(q+r)(q+w)].  (3)

This is the determinant formula for a two-vertex tetrahedral cap, after canceling the apparent p-q denominator. Thus repeated positive or negative heights cause no singularity.

Write f_i for the density at zero of sum_j c_ij E_j, with independent unit exponentials. Differentiating (3), or using the section-centroid first variation, gives

    P_1=P_2=(4s-1)/[4(s+2)], f_1=f_2=3/[4(s+2)],
    P_3=4(3s+2)/(s+2)^3, f_3=4s/(s+2)^3.           (4)

Put

    T=(4s-1)/3, U=(3s+2)/s,
    lambda=1/(2T+U)=3s/(8s^2+7s+6).

Define three rows and a fourth zero row by

    x_1=lambda(T1-c_1), x_2=lambda(T1-c_2),
    x_3=lambda(U1-c_3), x_4=0.                      (5)

They are column-stochastic because the margins sum to zero. Every entry in the first three rows is strictly positive. For the first two rows it is enough to prove T>q. Since p,q are the roots with sum s and product (1-s)/3, T-s/2=(5s-2)/6>0 and

    (T-s/2)^2-(q-p)^2/4=4(1-s)^2/9>0.

Thus T>q. For the third row U>2 is immediate. Column stochasticity and positivity imply that all these entries are also strictly less than one.

The actual capacity-minimizing thresholds are lambda T,lambda T,lambda U. Indeed T=P_1/f_1 and U=P_3/f_3 make threshold stationarity exact. Root-CDF concavity makes such a stationary threshold globally minimizing, and the positive-row uniqueness theorem makes it the unique minimum. Each cut is proper and has two strict vertices on each side.

Take objective weights

    a_1=P_1^(1/3), a_2=P_2^(1/3), a_3=P_3^(1/3),
    a_4=1/10.

Each full row then has weighted gradient exactly b, and

    sum_i a_i phi_3(x_i)=lambda(2T+U)=1.             (6)

The zero-row boundary has no first-order escape either. Its directional gain is a_4 phi_3(v)<=a_4 max v for v>=0. The weighted loss from the funding full rows is b dot v>=min_j b_j max v. Since C>1/8>1/10, the latter is strictly larger for v!=0. Thus all feasible first-order maximizing conditions hold, including arbitrary directions entering the zero row. This is not a claim of local maximality.

The three active rows are independent. Their difference is a nonzero multiple of (1,-1,0,0); their remaining two-dimensional common-pair span contains 1 and a nonconstant pair-constant vector. Hence their span is precisely

    V={v in R^4:v_3=v_4}.                            (7)

## 3. The two bad rows really have no positive curvature

Let H_i be the Hessian of the actual cap probability in raw margins at c_i. At c_1, on the two directions e=(1,-1,0,0) and z=(0,0,1,-1), exact differentiation of (3) gives

    e^T H_1 e=27(3s-2)/[8(s+2)^2],
    e^T H_1 z=0,
    z^T H_1 z=3/[8(s+2)].                            (8)

Both diagonal entries are positive. The gradient has equal coordinates within each pair, by (2); thus e,z are gradient-orthogonal. The three vectors e,z,c_1 form a basis of that three-dimensional tangent space. Homogeneity gives H_1 c_1=-grad P_1, so the remaining direction is a kernel there with zero cross terms. Therefore the fixed-through-b cap Hessian is positive semidefinite with only its radial kernel. The Schur-completed formula from `candidate a5d3d44181ebed82` implies that the fully optimized capacity Hessian is negative semidefinite with only its row-radial kernel. Row 2 has the same property.

For row 3, the two lower repeated entries and the two higher repeated entries have ratio 1/(s+1) in (1/2,3/5). The exact two-pair signature in `candidate 61582452a1450270` therefore gives exactly one positive direction, namely z. That direction is outside V in (7). Thus the joint-index inequality is saturated here: k=3 and total positive index one. A funding argument using only radial row changes cannot detect the saddle.

## 4. Exact optimal funding cost in the positive channel

First work with the unscaled rows T1-c_1,T1-c_2,U1-c_3. Multiplying a capacity Hessian by its objective weight removes the common fractional power of the cap probability. Along z, the common-shift Schur correction vanishes by symmetry, so the weighted second derivatives are exactly

    Q_1(z)=Q_2(z)=-1/6,
    Q_3(z)=s(6-s)/[6(s+2)^2].                       (9)

For the first two, (8) and T=P_1/f_1 give Q_1=-H_1[z,z]/(3f_1)=-1/6. For the third, the positive-pair sum has Beta(2,2) law with threshold u=s/(s+2). The cap second derivative in its pair-splitting direction is -2u^2(3-4u)/(s+2)^2. Multiplying by -1/(3f_3) gives the last expression in (9). The optimizing threshold has zero first variation by pair symmetry, so no threshold term has been omitted.

Give row 3 the direction z and fund it by -theta z in row 1 and -(1-theta)z in row 2. The total weighted second derivative is

    Q_3(z)-[theta^2+(1-theta)^2]/6.

Its maximum occurs at theta=1/2. This is also the best funding cost among arbitrary perturbations of the two bad rows whose sum is -z: their invariance under swapping coordinates 3 and 4 makes z Hessian-orthogonal to its pair-symmetric complement, and their Hessians are nonpositive on that complement. Hence any additional components can only increase the loss. Equal funding realizes the exact optimal cost 1/12.

The resulting surplus is

    Q_3(z)-1/12=(3s-2)(2-s)/[12(s+2)^2]>0.          (10)

Return to the actual rows (5). Homogeneity scales their Hessians by 1/lambda. Thus the genuinely feasible path

    x_1(epsilon)=x_1-epsilon z/2,
    x_2(epsilon)=x_2-epsilon z/2,
    x_3(epsilon)=x_3+epsilon z,
    x_4(epsilon)=0

has first derivative zero and second derivative exactly the positive number in (10) divided by lambda. All full entries stay positive for both signs of sufficiently small epsilon and every column sum is unchanged. Therefore every member of this family is a strict saddle, despite satisfying all first-order conditions and the joint-index bound.

## 5. One rational instance

Take p=1/5,q=1/2,s=7/10. Then lambda=35/247 and the active rows are

    (28,7,112,112)/494,
    (7,28,112,112)/494,
    (459,459,270,270)/494.

The common centroid is (10/27,10/27,7/54,7/54). The cap fractions are 1/6,1/6,16400/19683. In the unscaled channel the good-row curvature is 371/4374 and the exact two-row funding cost is 1/12, leaving 13/8748. In the actual stochastic coordinates the weighted second derivative is

    (247/35)(13/8748)=3211/306180>0.

The three distinct actual sections refute the proposed pencil-count reduction. Their exact positive compensated curvature supplies a different mechanism. It remains unproved here that an analogous compensation must hold for an arbitrary three-full-row stationary configuration with a common section centroid.

## 6. Complete reduction when the common section centroid has two equal pairs

The family above in fact exhausts the potentially remaining three-full-row maximizing configuration with a common centroid of the form (A,A,C,C), 2A+2C=1. This statement uses actual maximizing equations, not an asserted classification of every cap.

Consider a minimal-active positive-weight tetrahedral capacity maximizer with exactly three full rows. All minimizing thresholds are proper, unique and nondegenerate by the regularity and Schur theorems. All sections have one common centroid b. If every coordinate of b is at most 1/3, every full row has a captured central pair and positive capacity curvature; the joint-index bound k+sum p_i<=4 immediately excludes three such rows at k=3.

In the pair-symmetric case with a noncentral coordinate, relabel the pairs so A>1/3 and C<1/3. A triangular proper minimizing section could have at most one noncentral centroid coordinate. Thus all sections are strict quadrilaterals, and the same-side noncentral lemma forces their common unoriented split to be {1,2}|{3,4}.

We classify all sections of that split with centroid (A,A,C,C). Write their positive diagonal parameters as X,Y on the first side and Z,W on the second, and put

    T=X+Y+Z+W, M=XY, N=ZW,
    D=(X+Z)(Y+Z)(X+W)(Y+W)>0.

The exact centroid difference formulas factor as

    3(b_X-b_Y)=(X-Y)[NT^2-(M-N)^2]/(TD),
    3(b_Z-b_W)=(Z-W)[MT^2-(M-N)^2]/(TD).             (11)

If both pairs were unequal, the two bracket equations would imply M=N and then NT^2=0, impossible. Hence at least one pair is equal.

Suppose Z!=W. Then X=Y, and normalize X=Y=1. The second bracket equation is (Z+W+2)^2=(1-ZW)^2. Positivity rules out 1-ZW=Z+W+2; the other sign gives ZW=Z+W+3. Consequently the common centroid of Z,W equals

    (Z+W+3)/[3(Z+W+2)]>1/3,

contrary to C<1/3. Therefore Z=W. Normalize Z=W=1.

If X=Y=t, the centroid equation is A=t/[2(t+1)], giving one unique symmetric section. If X!=Y, the first bracket equation gives XY=X+Y+3. Put L=X+Y. Then

    A=(L+3)/[3(L+2)],
    L=3(1-2A)/(3A-1).

Distinct positive roots X,Y exist exactly when L>6, equivalently 1/3<A<3/8. They give precisely two asymmetric sections, exchanged by X and Y. At A=3/8 they coalesce with the symmetric section; at larger A no asymmetric section exists. Thus for A>=3/8 there is only one unoriented stationary section, and for 1/3<A<3/8 there are exactly the three sections of Section 1, with s=1/A-2.

The three active rows of a minimal-active maximizer are independent. Their raw margins c_i=t_i1-x_i sum to zero. If two margins were proportional, the third would be proportional too, and the rows would lie in the two-dimensional span of 1 and one margin, contradicting independence. Therefore all three unoriented sections must be distinct. This excludes A>=3/8.

For 1/3<A<3/8, use the canonical representatives (1). Their unique linear relation, up to an overall scalar, is c_1+c_2+c_3=0: the first-pair antisymmetric coordinate forces equal coefficients on c_1,c_2, and then the remaining coordinate fixes the third. Hence the actual three raw margins are a common positive multiple of these representatives, or a common positive multiple of all their negatives, after row relabeling.

In the globally reversed orientation, the two asymmetric rows capture the two central coordinates. Each has a positive capacity direction, so the joint-index bound excludes that orientation at k=3. In the displayed orientation, threshold stationarity fixes the thresholds to the same common multiple of T,T,U. Column sums fix that multiplier to lambda in (5). The maximizing weighted-gradient equations, after one common rescaling of the objective weights, fix the three full-row weights to P_1^(1/3),P_2^(1/3),P_3^(1/3). The zero row's weight is irrelevant to the feasible path of Section 4, since it remains zero. Thus the proposed maximizing configuration is exactly a member of the strictly improving family already proved above, a contradiction.

We conclude: a minimal-active tetrahedral weighted-capacity maximizer with exactly three full rows cannot have a common section centroid with two equal pairs. This closes that precise structural family. No perturbation or reduction of a general nonsymmetric common centroid to two equal pairs is asserted.

The independently audited root note `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)` also gives an attained global zero-diagonal competitor for every member of (5), with objective strictly greater than one. It uses h_3(P^(1/3),P^(1/3),Q^(1/3),0)=h_2(sqrt(P),sqrt(P),sqrt(Q))^(2/3) and a positive degree-six Bernstein certificate. The local funded-curvature proof and the pair-symmetric classification above do not depend on that alternative payment.
